title: Clarity: characters and actions
note: Joseph M. Williams taught that readers find prose clear when the main characters are grammatical subjects and their key actions are verbs, not nouns. Keep subjects short and close to their verbs. Begin a sentence with familiar (old) information and end with new, important information, where the stress falls.

read.title: Who is doing what?
text: Joseph Williams noticed that readers judge a sentence clear or murky largely by one thing: whether its grammar matches its story. Every sentence tells a small story with characters who do things. When the characters are the subjects and their actions are the verbs, readers follow easily.

Compare two versions. "The city's reconsideration of the zoning decision occurred after resident complaints" buries its characters (the city, the residents) inside modifiers and buries its actions (reconsider, complain) inside nouns. "After residents complained, the city reconsidered its zoning decision" puts characters in subject position and actions in verbs. It says the same thing, faster.

Williams added a principle about the flow from sentence to sentence. Readers like to start each sentence with something familiar and end with something new. If one sentence ends with "a new vaccine," the next reads best if it begins with "This vaccine" rather than with an unrelated fact. The end of a sentence, which Williams called the stress position, is where readers expect the most important new information.
To apply all this, ask of any confusing sentence: Who is doing what? Then make the who the subject and the what the verb.
